analysis.one_liner: Medicaid mandate for home care so disabled and older people can live at home instead of institutions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in any of its three committees and died when the Congress ended, with 12 cosponsors — all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make home and community-based services a required Medicaid benefit, ending the state-by-state waiting lists that leave hundreds of thousands of people with disabilities and older adults stranded without care or pushed into nursing homes. The federal government would pay the full cost of these services, states would have to pay direct care workers enough to keep them on the job, and new grant programs would recruit and train the workforce. Most provisions would take effect five years after passage.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities and older adults who need help with daily living — bathing, dressing, meals, transportation — and want to stay in their own homes rather than enter a nursing home or wait years on a state waiting list. Also the roughly 53 million unpaid family caregivers the bill cites, who would get respite and support services, and the low-paid direct care workforce the bill aims to stabilize with training grants and wage requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with disabilities, older adults, family caregivers

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state Medicaid program to cover home and community-based services — personal care, home health, private duty nursing, homemaking, transportation, respite, and caregiver support — as a mandatory benefit for people with functional impairments lasting at least 90 days.

The bill's stated purpose includes eliminating HCBS waiting lists, ending repeated state waiver applications, and preventing unnecessary institutionalization of people with disabilities and older adults.

Makes home and community-based services permanently protected against spousal impoverishment, so a spouse needing care isn't forced into poverty to qualify, and makes the Money Follows the Person program — which helps people move out of institutions — permanent.
Requires states, as a condition of full federal funding, to strengthen access, support family caregivers, and ensure payments are sufficient to make services actually available.

Creates a national technical assistance center and grant program to recruit, train, and retain direct care workers, whose field had a 45 percent turnover rate, and reclassifies direct support professionals in the federal occupational system.
Gives states new Medicaid eligibility categories for people needing home care, up to higher income levels, beginning at state option.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would pay 100 percent of the cost of home and community-based services — an open-ended entitlement with no stated dollar cap — and appropriate hundreds of millions for implementation, quality measurement, and workforce grants. States would take on administrative and planning work but see their Medicaid long-term care bills shifted largely to Washington. Nursing homes and other institutional providers would face competition as more people choose home care.

drawbacks.text: The bill directs the federal government to pay 100 percent of Medicaid home and community-based services costs and authorizes 'such sums as are necessary' for state implementation grants — an open-ended federal spending commitment with no ceiling in the text.
The mandatory coverage requirement does not begin until five years after enactment, so people on waiting lists would not see relief quickly even if it had passed.

Success depends on building a direct care workforce that currently has severe shortages and 45 percent annual turnover; without enough workers, a coverage mandate could create entitlements to services that don't exist in practice.
Ending the waiver system after five years dismantles the existing structure states rely on, a transition that would be operationally disruptive even for states that support the goal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and large: ending waiting lists and letting people receive care at home instead of institutions addresses one of the most persistent gaps in American long-term care, and the bill pairs the mandate with money to build the workforce. The honest cost is fiscal — full federal funding of an open-ended entitlement would be expensive, and the bill never received the cost estimate that would show how much. The five-year delay and the workforce shortage are the biggest design risks, but the bill attempts to address the workforce directly.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and to a Health subcommittee a week later, and none of them ever scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote — it simply died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the HCBS Access Act on March 9, 2023, with Rep. Jamaal Bowman, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Oversight committees.

On March 17, 2023, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and the action history shows no further activity — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the Congress.
The bill attracted 12 cosponsors, all House Democrats, and none of the three committees it was sent to acted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

A Senate companion approach had also been introduced in prior Congresses, and the home and community-based services expansion it sought was part of the same broader proposal Dingell had carried in earlier sessions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing homes and institutional care providers keep their patient base, states keep their current cost-sharing arrangement, and federal taxpayers avoid the large open-ended cost — while people stuck on home care waiting lists remain where they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Institutional care providers and the status quo

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and carried it through the Congress; it never advanced past committee referral.

for.name: 12 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee and House Oversight Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were House Democrats, and with Republicans holding a House majority, the bill never reached a hearing or vote; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and the direct care workforce
industries.note: The bill would make Medicaid home care a permanent mandatory benefit delivered largely through these agencies and workers, with states required to set payments 'sufficient' to ensure availability and grants to raise recruitment and retention. Their gain tracks with the public's: millions of people need this care and can't get it today, though the workers' notoriously low pay would only be addressed through state payment rules and grant programs, not a federal wage floor.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and institutional care providers
industries.note: A mandatory home care benefit would give people a real alternative to institutional placement, drawing Medicaid long-term care dollars toward home settings and away from nursing facilities. The bill also makes Money Follows the Person — a program that moves people out of institutions — permanent.

States would gain a 100 percent federal match on home and community-based services, shifting most of their long-term care costs to Washington, but would lose flexibility by having to cover a uniform benefit, submit implementation plans, and eventually retire their waiver systems.

The bill cites more than 53 million unpaid family caregivers and directs states to provide respite care and could allow paid family caregiving — direct financial relief for households currently providing complex care for free.
